title: Macbeth
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act I, Scene I — A desert place. Thunder and lightning.
openingText: FIRST WITCH: When shall we three meet again? In thunder, lightning, or in rain? SECOND WITCH: When the hurlyburly's done, when the battle's lost and won. THIRD WITCH: That will be ere the set of sun. FIRST WITCH: Where the place? SECOND WITCH: Upon the heath. THIRD WITCH: There to meet with Macbeth. ALL: Fair is foul, and foul is fair: hover through the fog and filthy air.
about:
Macbeth is a Scottish general who, on the prediction of three witches, kills his king and takes the throne. The rest of the play is what he does to keep it. He kills more, becomes paranoid, alienates everyone, and is finally killed himself. His wife — who pushed him into the first murder — descends into madness.

Written around 1606, Macbeth is the shortest of Shakespeare's tragedies and one of the most violent. It is also the most concentrated study of guilt in his work — what guilt does to the body and the mind. The play feels as though it is happening in real time, with consequences arriving faster than the people inside them can process.

angleCards.title: Did the witches cause this?
angleCards.text: They predict, but they do not command. Macbeth hears the prophecy and immediately starts planning. The question of whether they planted the idea or simply reflected it back runs through every act.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to ask whether the witches caused Macbeth's fall or simply named what was already there — and what that distinction means for how we think about fate and character.

angleCards.title: Ambition as a form of madness.
angleCards.text: By Act III, Macbeth is seeing daggers and ghosts. The play tracks how the first crime does not resolve the fear that produced it — it multiplies it. Watch what he imagines he needs to do next, and why.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read this as a study in how ambition warps perception — how Macbeth's imagination becomes his worst enemy once he has committed to a course.

angleCards.title: Lady Macbeth's undoing.
angleCards.text: She calls on spirits to unsex her and fill her with cruelty. It works — until it doesn't. Her disintegration runs in counterpoint to his: as he hardens, she collapses. The sleepwalking scene is the play's most devastating moment.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Lady Macbeth's arc — she begins stronger and more resolute than her husband, and ends broken. The play has something to say about what that costs.

angleCards.title: Good man or bad man revealed?
angleCards.text: We are told at the start that Macbeth is brave, loyal, and honoured. Then within two acts he is a murderer. The play keeps the question open: was this always in him, or did the witches and his wife unlock something that had no prior existence?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to ask whether Macbeth is a tragedy about a good man destroyed by circumstance or a bad man finally revealed — and whether Shakespeare gives us enough to decide.

cast.name: Macbeth
cast.description: A celebrated warrior with a conscience. He knows, before he acts, exactly what he is about to do and why it is wrong. He does it anyway. That lucidity is what makes him tragic rather than merely villainous.

cast.name: Lady Macbeth
cast.description: She is the harder of the two at the start. She goads, plans, and executes. But she cannot sustain the weight of what she has set in motion — and her collapse, when it comes, is total.

cast.name: The Three Witches
cast.description: They predict, they do not command. Everything they say comes true — but always in a way Macbeth did not anticipate. The play never fully explains what they are.

cast.name: Duncan
cast.description: The king — good, trusting, generous. He is killed in Act II before we know him well. The play makes his murder feel enormous despite giving him little stage time.

cast.name: Banquo
cast.description: Macbeth's closest companion, who heard the same prophecy and chose differently. His presence — and then his ghost — is the measure of what Macbeth has abandoned.

cast.name: Macduff
cast.description: The man the play has been preparing as the answer to Macbeth. He has suffered Macbeth's worst act personally, and arrives in Act V with a grief the play has earned.

acclaim.quote: There is an entire absence of comedy, nay, even of irony and philosophic contemplation in Macbeth, — the play being wholly and purely tragic.

whyItMatters.title: The Quickest Tragedy
whyItMatters.body: Macbeth is half the length of Hamlet and tighter than any of Shakespeare's other tragedies. Every scene tightens the screw. The play feels like it is happening in real time — guilt arriving faster than the mind can process it.

whyItMatters.title: Guilt as a Bodily Fact
whyItMatters.body: Lady Macbeth's "Out, damned spot," Macbeth seeing the dagger and the ghost — the play shows guilt as something the body and senses register before the mind admits. The interior life is staged as hallucination.

whyItMatters.title: The Witches' Question
whyItMatters.body: The witches appear to predict the future, but the play leaves open whether they cause it or only describe it. Macbeth might have done it without them. The play asks what we are responsible for when we are pushed by what we already want to hear.
